verses.note: The verse puts God before and outside everything that exists. Read as a full sentence, it says the universe has a beginning and that God is its cause; read as a time clause, it still makes God the one who acts on the world. Either way nothing in heaven or earth shares his status.
God names the day and the night. In the ancient world naming expressed authority, so even darkness, which neighboring peoples feared, has its name and place from God.

God does not make a finished, static world but a fruitful one, with seed carrying life forward. Creation has its own God-given capacities, which is why Scripture can praise God both for making the world and for sustaining its seasons.

God's blessing on animals shows that his care reaches beyond humanity. Scripture later has the sea creatures praising God (Psalm 148:7) and Jesus saying that not one sparrow falls apart from the Father (Matthew 10:29).

The whole created order, material and embodied, is very good in God's sight. Paul draws on this when he rejects teachers who forbid marriage and foods, saying everything God created is good (1 Timothy 4:4).

The verse insists that creation was brought to completion. The world as God made it lacked nothing it needed to be good, which is why later disorder in Genesis is presented as damage to a finished work, not as a stage in an unfinished one.

By naming rivers that Israel knew, the text insists that Eden belongs to the same real world as Assyria and the Euphrates. The garden story is not set in a mythic nowhere; it is the beginning of human history on this earth.

The echo of 1:31 shows that corruption is a reversal of creation's goodness, not a flaw in its making. The world God saw as very good is the same world he now sees ruined, and the difference is what creatures did with it.

On the second day God separated the waters above from the waters below; on the third he gathered the seas so that dry land appeared. Verse 11 releases both at once. The flood is creation running backward, and it shows that the world's order holds only because God holds it (Psalm 104:9, Jeremiah 5:22).

The ark is a small creation carried through the collapse of the large one. The same categories God created ‘according to their kinds’ are preserved by kind, so that the world after the flood will be a continuation of the first creation, not a replacement.

The wind over the waters and the drying land that follows repeat the opening of Genesis 1. Judgment has returned the earth almost to the watery state of 1:2, and God begins again from there, which shows that his purpose for creation outlasts his judgment on it.

The blessing that went out to living creatures in Genesis 1 is spoken again over the animals leaving the ark. God's intention for a full and teeming earth was interrupted by judgment but not withdrawn.

Food is still received as God's gift. Paul draws on this pattern when he insists that nothing God created is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving (1 Timothy 4:3-5), and the New Testament's declaration that all foods are clean (Mark 7:19) returns to the breadth of this grant.

The blessing names the whole created order, heaven above, the deep below, and the body's power to bear and nurse, and puts all of it in the hand of the God of Jacob. Fertility is God's gift, not the domain of the fertility gods of Canaan.

By echoing Genesis 1:28, the verse presents Israel as the place where God's original blessing on humanity is being carried forward. What God intended for the whole human race takes shape first in one family.

God claims to be the maker of every human body, including bodies that cannot speak, hear, or see. The verse does not explain why people differ in ability, but it refuses to place any person outside God's making and purpose, a point Jesus makes about the man born blind (John 9:1-3).
